props.title: King of Kings
props.initialSlug: Epic retelling of Jesus Christ's life and ministry

sections.content: King of Kings (1961) stands as a pivotal Biblical epic that redefined how Jesus Christ was portrayed on screen. Unlike Cecil B. DeMille's reverential The Ten Commandments (1956), director Nicholas Ray took a more humanistic approach, with Jeffrey Hunter presenting a younger, more accessible Jesus. The film arrived during Hollywood's fascination with religious epics, following Ben-Hur (1959) and preceding The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965), but distinguished itself through its focus on the political tensions of Roman-occupied Judea.

sections.content: Ray's direction in King of Kings brought unprecedented psychological depth to Biblical characters. Barabbas becomes a complex revolutionary rather than a simple villain, while Judas's betrayal carries political weight beyond mere greed. This approach influenced later religious films like Jesus Christ Superstar (1973) and The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), which similarly explored the human dimensions of divine stories.

The film's epic scale, captured in Super Technirama 70, set new standards for Biblical spectacle. Miklos Rozsa's magnificent score and the extensive use of Spanish locations created a sense of authenticity that later epics like The Bible: In the Beginning... (1966) would attempt to match. Modern religious epics like The Passion of the Christ (2004) still draw from Ray's groundbreaking mix of intimacy and grandeur. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Biblical Epics Post-King of Kings

sections.content: The influence of King of Kings resonates through subsequent Biblical adaptations. Films like The Gospel According to St. Matthew (1964) adopted its more grounded approach, while Jesus of Nazareth (1977) expanded on its historical context. Modern interpretations like Mary Magdalene (2018) continue this tradition of humanizing Biblical figures while maintaining spiritual significance.
